beginNamedQueryTransaction.doc: Begins a new database transaction using named queries. Database transactions are used to execute multiple queries in an atomic fashion. After executing queries, you must either commit the transaction to have your changes take effect, or rollback the transaction which will make all operations since the last commit not take place. The transaction is given a new unique string code, which is then returned. You can then use this code  as the tx argument for other system.db.* function calls to execute various types of queries using this transaction. All queries in the transaction must be in the same project and same database.

beginTransaction.doc:
Begins a new database transaction. Database transactions are used to execute multiple queries in an atomic fashion. After executing queries, you must either commit the transaction to have your changes take effect, or rollback the transaction which will make all operations since the last commit not take place. The transaction is given a new unique string code, which is then returned. You can then use this code as the tx argument for other system.db.* function calls to execute various types of queries using this transaction.

An open transaction consumes one database connection until it is closed. Because leaving connections open indefinitely would exhaust the connection pool, each transaction is given a timeout. Each time the transaction is used, the timeout timer is reset. For example, if you make a transaction with a timeout of one minute, you must use that transaction at least once a minute. If a transaction is detected to have timed out, it will be automatically closed and its transaction id will no longer be valid.

params.doc: The name of the database connection to execute against. If omitted or "", the project's default database connection will be used.
params.name: database

params.doc: The transaction isolation level to use. Use one of the four constants: <tt>system.db.READ_COMMITTED</tt>, <tt>system.db.READ_UNCOMMITTED</tt>, <tt>system.db.REPEATABLE_READ</tt>, or <tt>system.db.SERIALIZABLE</tt>
params.name: isolationLevel

params.doc: The amount of time, in milliseconds, that this connection is allowed to remain open without being used. Timeout counter is reset any time a query or call is executed against the transaction, or when committed or rolled-back.
params.name: timeout

beginTransaction.returns: The new transaction ID. You'll use this ID as the "tx" argument for all other calls to have them execute against this transaction.

runPrepQuery.doc:
Runs a prepared statement against the database, returning the results in a PyDataset. Prepared statements use the question-mark character (?) as a placeholder in the query where any dynamic arguments would go,and then use a list of values to provide real information for those arguments. Make sure that the length of your argument array matches the number of question-mark placeholders in your query. This call should be used for SELECT queries.

This is a useful alternative to system.db.runQuery because it allows values in the WHERE clause, JOIN clause, and other clauses to be specified without having to turn those values into strings. This is safer because it protects against a problem known as a SQL injection attack, where a user can input data that affects the query's semantics.

This is a useful alternative to system.db.runUpdateQuery because it allows values in the WHERE clause, JOIN clause, and other clauses to be specified without having to turn those values into strings. A "Request" object, which provides:
  • get() - Block until result is available, throws error on failure.
  • cancel() - attempt to cancel the request.
  • onSuccess(func) - sets the onSuccess function.
  • onFailure(func) - sets the onFailure function.
  • block() - Like get(), but returns a boolean indicating success instead of throwing an exception. If false, the caller can then call getError() to get the exception object.
  • getError() - returns the exception encountered, if the request failed.
